https://www.indcatholicnews.com/news/556.text: Home News UK & Ireland US & Canada World Obituaries & Tributes Justice, Peace & Environment Education Youth & Young Adults Reflections Reflections & Homilies Viewpoint Letters Blogs Arts & Culture Gospel in Art Art, Theatre, Music & Shows Films, TV & Radio Books Poetry Travel Listings Forthcoming Events Regular Events Classified Ads Jobs Courses & Voluntary Work Retreat, Spirituality and Pilgrimage Centres Businesses, Accommodation & Travel Prayers Contact Resources Links About Source: Polish Catholic Mission The Polish Catholic Mission said in a statement today: "We received with deep sorrow the news that on August 17, 2026, at the age of 50 and after 25 years of priesthood, Fr Dariusz Mazur, parish priest of the Parish of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul in Zawad, passed away. Fr Dariusz served the Polish community in Great Britain for many years, working for many years in the Polish Catholic Mission in England and Wales. His last place of service in Great Britain was the Polish Parish in Gloucester and Cheltenham. He returned to Poland a year ago. We remember his many years of pastoral service among the Polish community and the good deeds he left behind in the communities he entrusted to him. Today, 19 August, a Funeral Mass was held in the Parish of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul in Zawad presided over by Abbot Wacław Depo, Metropolitan of Częstochowa. On Thursday, 20 August 20, 2026, at 12 noon there will be a Funeral Mass in the Parish of St Joseph the Worker in Pustkowo (between Dębic and Mielce), in the Tarnowskie diocese, presided by Fr Antoni Długosz. After the Mass, the body of the late Fr Dariusz will be laid to rest in the family cemetery at the parish cemetery. We ask the priests and faithful of the Polish Catholic Mission in England and Wales to pray for our deceased colleague and chaplain. Grant him eternal rest, O Lord, and may eternal light shine upon him. May he rest in eternal peace. Amen." http://www.rightspeak.net/2026/09/when-g.text: U.S. General Elections Central Three Percenters (III%ers) Right Speak (FB) #MASA (Make America Safe Again) Saturday, September 12, 2026 When Genocide Apologists Put America on Trial for Genocide: And What It Can Teach Us About Today’s Fake Genocides After selling the lie that Israel’s military campaign against Hamas after Oct 7 was genocide, leftists have pivoted to claiming that Cuba is the new Gaza and is also being genocided. The Democratic Socialists of America recently issued a statement praising the murderous Cuban dictator Fidel Castro and accusing Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is of Cuban heritage, of waging a “genocidal war against the Cuban people” by maintaining the embargo. The big lie of the Gaza ‘genocide’ had been based in part on falsely accusing Israel of starving the enemy population in the Hamas territory (in reality, the UN, which helped push the lie, had refused to deliver much of the food and admitted that 95% of its aid trucks were “intercepted”.) After arguing that Israel had committed genocide by not sufficiently delivering food to Hamas, the DSA and some of the same players are arguing that America is committing genocide in Cuba by not allowing commercial dealings with the Communist dictatorship. Similar genocide smears had been hurled at the United States for imposing sanctions on Saddam Hussein’s Iraq whose regime, like that of Castro, had engaged in the actual mass murder of its own people. America did not commit genocide in Cuba, but the Castro regime imprisoned 100,000 people in prisons and camps and killed between 15,000 and 17,000 people . The DSA cheers on these crimes today while falsely accusing America of genocide in order to bail out the Cuban regime. But it’s certainly not the first time that America and its allies were falsely accused of genocide by leftist activists who were complicit in covering up actual genocide by their Communist allies. While leftists have falsely accused America of committing genocide in every war from the Korean War (“the American forces are guilty of the crime of Genocide” – International Association of Democratic Lawyers) to the Iraq War (“an act of genocide” – Workers World), the high point of the genocide lie came during the Vietnam War where the ‘International War Crimes Tribunal’ was convened by intellectuals to convict America of the crime of genocide. In 1951, the Civil Rights Congress, a Communist front group, and Paul Robeson, a Stalinist, who had defended a regime that murdered millions, had presented We Charge Genocide, a petition to the UN accusing America of genocide in Korea and domestically through racism. During this same period, there were an estimated 2.5 million prisoners in Stalin’s gulag camps. The 1966 tribunal was a slicker arrangement fronted by Bertrand Russell, whose occasional liberal anti-Communism had veered towards anti-Americanism, but was funded by Ho Chi Minh and the tribunal was dominated by Communists, Marxists and their allies including a Cuban official, Kwame Ture of the Black Panther Party and French ‘philosopher’ Jean-Paul Sartre. Sartre was appointed as the president of the International War Crimes Tribunal and did much of the work indicting America for genocide even while an actual genocide was being plotted in Viet Cong camps by Communist Cambodians who had been inspired by Sartre’s works during their time in exile in France to implement what would become the Cambodian genocide. By 1966, the Khmer Rouge had secured the support of the Chinese Communist regime, which was far more genocidally murderous than Vietnam’s Communists, and a decade later began a Communist genocide that took the lives of over 2 million people even as American and European socialists, and some members of the tribunal, lied and tried to cover up their crimes. Sartre had already been an enthusiastic apologist for the massacres of both Stalin and Mao. “A revolutionary regime must rid itself of a certain number of individuals who threaten it, and I see no other way than death. One can always escape from prison,” Sartre had argued in a 1973 interview, suggesting that during the French Revolution, “the revolutionaries of 1793 probably didn’t kill enough and thus unconsciously facilitated a return to order, and then the Restoration.” “It was not our duty to write about Soviet labor camps,” Sartre had argued about Soviet genocide back in 1950. “We were free to remain aloof from the quarrel over the nature of this system, provided no events of sociological significance had occurred.” The deaths of 3 million people were not of sociological significance to Sartre: after all Lenin and Stalin had not made the same mistake as the French revolutionaries by not killing enough. When Soviet tanks entered Budapest, Sartre criticised the scale of the massacres, but argued that the Hungarians had brought it on themselves by allying with “reactionary elements” so that “the reappearance of conservative parties made the Russian presence (not brutal intervention) in Hungary practically necessary” and that really “the most enormous mistake was probably Khrushchev’s report” denouncing Stalin because, he argued, “the detailed exposition of all the crimes of a sacred figure, who represented the regime for so long, is madness”. After visiting the USSR in 1954, Sartre claimed in an interview that there is a “complete freedom of criticism” in the USSR and “the Soviet citizen criticizes more and in a much more effective way” than Europeans do. His hosts plied him with so much food and drink that he became ill from boozing and claimed that by 1960, “the average standard of living in the USSR will be 30 to 40% higher than ours”. In reality, by the 1960s, there were food protests in the USSR resulting in more domestic repression including the Novocherkassk massacre in 1962. Like many socialists, Sartre justified everything, including his lies and those of the regime, because he argued that, “Communism must be judged on its intentions and not solely on its actions.” He laid out his position with painful clarity when he used this to explain why Communist atrocities were understandable, but America must always be condemned. “It is possible that there are a million deportees in certain countries occupied by the Russians. Fine. I am told this: we must protest strongly against this. On the other hand, I am told: it is very distressing that a black man was lynched in Alabama, for example. But he is a black man. We have one here and a million over there.” Sartre, however, contended that America, not the Soviet Union must be condemned because “if this deportation takes place, it is profoundly reprehensible, but it is a means to an end” while the lynching is “a mode of oppression.” The killing of millions of people in the USSR, China (“nowhere have I ever witnessed such solidarity”), and in Cambodia was a means to an end and that end was socialism. Sartre glorified murderous dictatorships including the “spiritual revolution” in Iran because he agreed with their objectives while smearing America as genocidal because he disagreed with ours. Sartre’s ‘conviction’ of the United States for committing genocide in Vietnam rested on his contention that all the Vietnamese (or all the ones he cared about) were Communists and thus “the only anti-guerrilla strategy which will be effective is the destruction of that people, in other words, the civilians, women and children.” American imperialists were committing genocide “as a warning to all humanity” (by humanity, Sartre once again meant Communists), and failing to fight with the Viet Cong against American capitalism also “amounts to genocide”. Most revealingly, if the Americans were to defeat the Communists, they would “rebuild the DRV with mountains of dollars” and “this would mean that they would destroy, with their private investments or conditional loans, all the economic basis of socialism. That, too, is genocide.” Genocide, to Sartre, was the defeat of socialism in general and Communism specifically. Sartre, like many leftists, did not have a problem with the murder of millions of people. He did not use the term ‘genocide’ to describe the killing of millions under Communism, only to describe the defeat of Communism and everything that the socialists stood for. ---> READ MORE HERE Post a Comment Our Community Blog: RIGHT SPEAK Chat: Search Right Speak Blog Archive: Right Speak tweets Blogger's (No. Posts) -Areté (12) -BOSMAN (31232) -DanL (81) -Diana Rae (51) -Diane Sori (981) -Doug NYC GOP (88) -Granny T (10) -JohnG (144) -Katrina L. Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/Getty View image in fullscreen A tree brought down by Storm Austen blocks the pavement in Falmouth, Cornwall, on Friday. Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/Getty Extreme weather Thousands of homes without power as Storm Austen hits south-west England Dozens of schools in Cornwall also affected as Storm Boelo heads for Scotland, Northern Ireland and north of England Jamie Grierson and Yassin El-Moudden Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.30 EDT First published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 07.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Thousands of homes are without power and schools were closed as the first named storm of the year hit UK shores. Storm Austen brought severe conditions to parts of the south-west, with a gust of 76mph recorded at St Mary’s airport on the Isles of Scilly on Friday morning. Just before 11am, more than 16,000 homes in the south-west were without power, according to National Grid. Dozens of schools across Cornwall were forced to delay their opening, while others did not open at all. Flights were disrupted at airports in the south-west and on the Channel Islands, and passengers were being advised to check the status of their flight before travelling. Guernsey airport’s duty manager, Steve Ford, confirmed that normal service was not expected to resume before Saturday morning, with most of the fleet having been stranded on the UK mainland. The Dutch flag carrier, KLM, cancelled dozens of its scheduled flights for Friday and Saturday. Images showed part of Brighton’s West Pier falling into the sea after it was battered by wind and waves. The pier, first opened in 1866, has grown increasingly derelict since it closed to the public in 1975, with storms and fires destroying much of what remained. English Heritage has previously declared the structure beyond repair. National Rail reported severe disruption across the rail network, with cancellations across England , Wales and Scotland. Forecasters have put an additional amber weather warning for wind in place from Saturday into Sunday as the second named storm of the year, Boelo, heads in. Speaking to reporters on Friday, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “We potentially are facing a winter of greater flooding, so it’s about recognising all of those risks and taking action.” View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham speaking at a wildfires summit in Aintree, Liverpool, on Friday. Photograph: WPA/Getty A government campaign aimed at urging people to stock supplies of food and essentials in case of multi-day emergencies made headlines overnight. Burnham was asked whether the government was playing catchup with civil preparedness as he attended a summit organised to learn from the summer’s record wildfires. He answered: “No. We are having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we’re living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common. “We’re in a situation today where the UK is facing storms, and obviously we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now. “It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments [and] we are having that conversation about resilience. That’s why we’re holding this summit today, it’s why we’re putting the guidance out to the public.” National Grid said engineers had restored power to more than 12,000 properties affected by Storm Austen by 8am on Friday. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion A Met Office amber warning for wind covering Cornwall, Devon and the Isles of Scilly was issued on Wednesday, taking effect on Friday from 1am until 10am. View image in fullscreen Storm Austen hits Newhaven in East Sussex. Photograph: Toby Melville/Reuters The Met Office has now issued a 24-hour amber warning for wind from Storm Boelo from 9pm on Saturday, covering Scotland, the north coast of Northern Ireland, and Cumbria and Northumberland in the north of England. The forecaster said gusts of up to 80mph could hit exposed coastal areas, with winds of 60-70mph widespread elsewhere, and it warned of danger to life from flying debris. It said there was also a “good chance” of power cuts, damage to buildings, trees being uprooted and travel disruption. In anticipation of Storm Boelo, train lines in parts of northern and western Scotland are scheduled to close early at the weekend. Services south and west of Kilwinning in North Ayrshire and the Oban and Mallaig lines will shut on Saturday evening, while the line between Kyle of Lochalsh and Achnashellach in the Highlands will be out of service on Sunday. Trains are expected to run at reduced speed elsewhere in the country. The Republic of Ireland’s weather agency, Met Éireann, issued six warnings of varying severity for Saturday, mostly affecting counties along the west coast. https://business-review.eu/property/one-.text: One United Properties acquires land in Floreasca for new residential‑led mixed-use tower One United Properties (BVB: ONE), Romania’s leading investor and developer of sustainable residential, mixed-use, and office real estate projects, announces the acquisition of a 5,755 sqm plot of land at 110-112 Barbu Văcărescu Street. The company plans to develop a mixed-use tower on the site, in an area that pairs proximity to nature with easy access to Bucharest’s main business district. The transaction amount is EUR 10 million. According to the preliminary design concept, the building will include four basement levels, a ground floor, and 25 upper floors, with an above-ground gross built area of approximately 25,900 sqm. At more than 100 meters tall, the tower will be one of the tallest residential buildings in Romania. The lower floors will include retail and office space, with a range of services and amenities. Besides housing, the project will feature shops, workspaces, and 2,000 sqm of green space to the area. One United Properties will run an international architecture competition for the tower’s design, with the aim of delivering an iconic building for the city. The company took the same approach for One City District, whose masterplan will be designed by French architect Jean-Michel Wilmotte. “We chose this site for its location and for the way it complements our investments in Floreasca-Barbu Văcărescu. We have developed homes and offices here, and through One Gallery we are bringing in restaurants, wellness facilities, and event spaces. The synergy between these functions creates value: nearby services add to the appeal of the new project, while future residents will broaden the customer base of local businesses. We also care about what this investment brings to the community: more services within walking distance, places to meet, and street-level spaces for everyone in the neighborhood to enjoy. These benefits will be written into the brief for the international architecture competition, in which we will be looking for a design that makes the most of the site’s position and views, paying as much attention to the tower’s silhouette as to the way the building opens up to the street,” said Andrei Diaconescu, co-founder and co-CEO of One United Properties. Read more about SPEEDWELL expands services mix at PALTIM project in Timisoara with dental college and medical clinics read more The acquisition expands the company’s presence in a part of the Romanian capital where it has been building for more than a decade, and where its portfolio includes established landmarks such as One Floreasca City, One Gallery, One Floreasca Towers, and One Verdi Park. In the Floreasca – Barbu Văcărescu area, ONE has completed developments with a combined gross development value of around EUR 536 million. A further portfolio with a gross development value of approximately EUR 360 million is under construction in the same area, including One Floreasca Sunset, One Peninsula, and One Floreasca Club. The development planned for the newly acquired site will add another EUR 130 million in gross development value. The newly acquired site is a few minutes’ walk from One Gallery, the former Ford Hall restored by ONE, which is home to Marketta Food Hall, one of the largest food halls in the region, alongside offices, event spaces, and a private club dedicated to health, wellness, and longevity. The neighborhood is well connected to the rest of the city, with quick access to Bucharest’s northern office hub and the A3 motorway. Access was recently improved further by the upgrade of the tram line along Barbu Văcărescu, which reopened in March 2026 and offers a direct link to Băneasa Airport and Bucur Obor. https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text: Listen (3 mins) Save Share Cost of living protests hit Belgium, Italy, Portugal and France on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google Italian demonstrators clash with police at Piazza Duomo in Milan on Saturday [Piero Cruciatti/AFP] By Al Jazeera Staff , AFP , AP and Reuters Published On 17 Oct 2026 17 Oct 2026 Hundreds of thousands of Europeans have taken to the streets in separate, uncoordinated demonstrations to protest against the rising cost of living in their countries. Saturday’s wave of unrest in Belgium, France, Italy and Portugal has put pressure on governments across the European Union. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Albanian police fire rubber bullets as protests against Rama escalate list 2 of 3 Tear gas and unrest as hundreds of thousands protest for reforms in France list 3 of 3 Buildings and cars set on fire as cost of living protests rock France end of list France experienced one of its most turbulent days of protests in decades, with more than 550,000 people joining demonstrations, according to the Ministry of Interior, and police facing off with protesters across the country. The marches, which followed weeks of student protests, degenerated into clashes, looting and fires after violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 1,200 people were arrested and 150 police officers were hurt. “It’s a miracle the toll wasn’t higher,” he said as he visited officers deployed in central Paris. Dozens of shops were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg, the French news agency AFP reported. Whole streets in the capital “have been devastated”, Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said. A fire set by masked protesters in Limoges largely destroyed the more than 140-year-old town hall, while city halls in Marseille and Lille were broken into and vandalised. In Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office. President Emmanuel Macron said on X that those responsible would be “prosecuted and punished”. In Belgium’s capital, Brussels – which has already seen weeks of protests by students against university registration fees – police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters, whom they accused of launching missiles at them and setting fires. Advertisement In Liege, a smaller city east of Brussels, police also deployed water cannon to break up demonstrations. Police did not say how many people attended. Meanwhile, in the Portuguese capital of Lisbon, an estimated tens of thousands of protesters marched against the cost of living crisis, low wages and an inability to access housing in major cities. House prices in Portugal have more than doubled ⁠⁠since 2017, while rents for new leases have increased nearly as much. Portuguese Parliamentary Affairs Minister Carlos ‌‌Abreu ‌‌Amorim said on Friday that the “government will not yield to shouts from the street”. Protesters said their leaders are “out of touch” with the problem. Italy In Milan, rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire in the city centre, emptying Piazza del Duomo and a luxury arcade that would usually be full of shoppers. A march against wars and rising living costs began peacefully, but masked protesters threw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and set fire to barricades made from bar tables. Police used water cannon and tear gas to disperse the crowds. At least two police officers were injured, and about 50 demonstrators, many of them minors, were detained, the Italian LaPresse news agency reported. Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the violence. “Demonstrating is a right. Setting our cities ablaze is not,” she wrote on X, blaming “hooligans who exploit demonstrations to sow chaos”. Milan’s centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, said “the reasons for the protests were understandable. The violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city are not justifiable.” In Bologna, police also reported that, alongside peaceful rallies, protesters threw stones and clashed with officers. Demonstrators in Lisbon set up tents to protest against the housing shortage, soaring rents and low wages [Filipe Amorim/AFP] French protests spill over Although protests in the other countries did not reach the same scale as the rallies in France, they may be a sign of discontent spilling over, Alberto Alemanno, professor of EU law and policy at HEC Paris Business School, told Al Jazeera. “France is the epicentre of this movement … and there are signs now that this is spreading beyond France,” Alemanno said. He said Saturday’s protests may not be the last in many of these countries and new hotspots could emerge. In Greece, Germany, and Austria, the “early stages” of a movement are emerging, with mobilisation expected “in the coming week”, he said. Advertisement They are not a single movement, he explained, but several protests happening at the same time, with some “shared grievances”: underfunded education, rising living costs and, for students, uncertain prospects after graduation. The unrest comes at a crucial time for Europe, Alemanno said, as the continent prepares for an “unprecedented super-cycle of national elections” in the coming 12 months, with votes scheduled in Spain, France, Italy and Poland. “Inevitably, all these protests, all these mobilisations, are going to be at the centre of the political conversation,” Alemanno said. Riot police fire water cannon during a youth protest in Brussels [Nicolas Maeterlinck/AFP]

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: Residents and their cat evacuated from the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky react on arrival at an undisclosed location in Ukraine on Saturday. Photograph: Genya Savilov/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Residents and their cat evacuated from the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky react on arrival at an undisclosed location in Ukraine on Saturday. Photograph: Genya Savilov/AFP/Getty Images Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Oleshky truce shows de-escalation is possible, says Zelenskyy Ukrainian president says Moscow must be shown that support for Kyiv will not diminish; US says interest also growing for limited Black Sea ceasefire. What we know on day 1,712 Guardian staff and agencies Sun 1 Nov 2026 00.17 EDT Last modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 02.55 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Oleshky ceasefire shows that de-escalation steps with Russia are possible, while the US says there is growing interest for a truce in the Black Sea. Zelenskyy said the humanitarian operation in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky “clearly demonstrates that de-escalation steps are possible when Russia is the one put in a position where it has to take steps toward de-escalation”. The Ukrainian president also said at a news conference with his Turkish counterpart, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, in Istanbul on Saturday: “Strong decisions are needed to bring peace. At every level, Russia must be sent signals that there is no alternative to peace and that support for Ukraine will not diminish. This is all the more important given that a humanitarian operation took place in Oleshky, in the Kherson region, over the past few days.” In the US, the secretary of state said there was growing interest in the international community in facilitating a limited ceasefire in the Black Sea to ensure unfettered energy and grain shipments by Russia and Ukraine. Marco Rubio said the US was reviewing proposals by Turkey and India to get grain shipments moving, even ⁠as the US continued to press ⁠for a broader negotiated settlement of the war. There was growing interest – if not momentum – in partial deals such as halting attacks on ships carrying grain and, in some ​cases, energy in the Black Sea, Rubio said ⁠on Saturday. “This is threatening the world for food security and ‌some energy security as well,” he told reporters in Atlanta after a ‌two-day G20 foreign ministers’ meeting that involved Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov despite objections from European and Canadian leaders . Zelenskyy said at the Istanbul news conference that he and Erdoğan had discussed the prospects of holding trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in early November, as well as other possibilities “including ways to involve Türkiye and all of Europe”. Erdoğan, meanwhile, said attacks aimed at civilian vessels in the Black Sea were unacceptable, urging Russia and Ukraine to “act responsibly”. “We cannot accept these attacks under any circumstances, regardless of who carries them out or what justification is offered.” Talks aimed at restoring the safety of navigation in the Black Sea would continue, Erdoğan added. Zelenskyy accused Russia of making the situation in the Black Sea difficult. In Ukraine, evacuees from Oleshky were reunited with loved ones after crossing into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday amid the US-brokered localised ceasefire. Evacuees wrapped in Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border to be reunited with family members. Evacuees told Agence France-Presse that some residents had to eat grass and dogs to survive and that their rescue following a humanitarian truce was a “blessing”. “People were cooking grass. They’d grow it as there was nothing to eat,” said Valera, a 29-year-old former resident who did not give his last name. “Lots of people were blown up. There were piles of bodies on the roads, loads of cars. In short, it was brutal ... terrifying.” The truce in the southern Kherson region was expected to continue until Sunday evening. Russia said on Sunday a drone had struck an “industrial enterprise” east of Moscow overnight, after Ukraine claimed it had hit a major oil refinery . Gleb Nikitin, governor of Nizhny Novgorod region, reported a “massive drone attack” during the night in which an “industrial enterprise in the Kstovo district sustained significant damage”. Preliminary information suggested there were no casualties, he added, without specifying the plant’s activities. Ukrainian media reported an attack on the Kstovo oil refinery, calling it “one of Russia’s largest oil refineries, producing fuel and lubricants”. On Saturday Ukraine’s ‌general staff said the military hit a major missile ⁠fuel ⁠producer in ​Russia’s Rostov region overnight, ⁠causing a fire and damaging four ⁠production facilities.
